sweptAxes.result: NEW LEADER. $4077.96 on 148 trades at 13.54% DD -- level with buy-and-hold BTC ($4105.94) at roughly a quarter of its 52.06% drawdown.

Built the last idea from the literature search: rank the universe by trailing Sharpe and trade only the leaders. It does NOT help returns. Tighter selection monotonically lowers the balance and lowers the drawdown, the same risk/return dial every other filter turned out to be: topN 12 gives $3685.85 at 10.96% DD, topN 3 gives $2363.77 at 7.81%. The nominal new best, topN 20 of 29 pairs at $4175.64, filters almost nothing -- it drops 5 trades of 148 for +2.4%, which is noise at this sample size, not selection working.

sweptAxes.axis: higherTfs x alignMode x swing window
sweptAxes.result: Adding a higher timeframe to the breakout leader collapses it: 143 trades to 71, $4175.64 to $1289.87. The cause is not alignment -- alignMode and n were flagged INERT by the new detector, byte-identical across every value. It is that trendSrc is the HIGHEST timeframe present, so a 3-day series turns the 200-period MA gate into a 600-day lookback. Supplying a higher timeframe is not an alignment-only change.

sweptAxes.axis: alignMode where it is actually wired
sweptAxes.result: bos and anticipate are the only modes that consult alignMode, and only with a higher timeframe present. Swept there it genuinely binds -- anticipate on a weekly anchor gives 237 trades/$2390 at alignMode none against 162/$2539 at first -- but nothing beats the leader. Best is $3833.05 (anticipate, 3-day anchor, alignMode none, trendMa 20) at a 21.77% drawdown. 'first' and 'all' are identical with a single higher timeframe, as they must be.

Raw sweep runs to $16,138 at volTarget 0.10 / clamp 5, and that number is LEVERAGE -- the universe's median trade sits at 5.55% ATR, so a 10% target scales every bet up and deploys 3.7x the risk. Risk-matched (equity.mjs riskMatchedRiskPct holds mean deployed risk at 0.5%) the real answer is $5087 against $4175.64 flat, at 13.41% drawdown against 13.54% -- and it is FLAT across volTarget 0.03-0.10 at any clamp >= 3. That plateau is the point: once the clamp is loose the weights are just proportional to 1/ATR% and the level cancels, so there is one structural decision here and no threshold to fit. First such change in the campaign.

Filling on the NEXT bar's open instead of the signal bar's close IMPROVES the result: $4874.70 against $4595.23, and it wins on every robustness margin -- worst-pair-out $3723 vs $3480, full-history $3636 vs $3431, drop-ten-best $1125 vs $1049, and higher mean R in all three years. Mechanically it declines to buy the close of the breakout day, which is the top of that day's move. Two bars collapses to $2305, so this is a discontinuity rather than a curve. Adopted, because it is both the more realistic assumption and the better one. feeBufferPct barely matters below 0.05.

The strongest evidence so far that the result is not a cost-model artifact. At 3x the modelled fee (2.4% vs 0.8%) AND 40x the modelled slippage (2% vs 0.05%) the strategy still ends at $2580.11, above the $1419.93 equal-weight basket. At 2x fees and 10x slippage it is $3458.78. It degrades smoothly and stays positive across the whole grid.

Capping simultaneous positions at 3 and raising per-position risk to 1% gives $5160.44 at an 8.96% drawdown, against the unlimited book's $4874.70 at 12.94%. More return, less drawdown, and LESS capital at risk at the peak: 3 x 1% = 3% against 19 x 0.5% = 9.5%. The nineteen concurrent longs were largely the same bet nineteen times.

Every one of 27 configurations loses. Best $993.06 at a 49.48% drawdown. Run without a trend gate, because the 'ma' gate as written asks whether price is ABOVE its average -- the wrong condition for a short.

leader.name: walk-forward-endorsed
leader.why: Every component chosen by a training-only search. btcRegime 50 is the newest: it had never actually been OFFERED to the walk-forward -- the filter grid held only null, atrPctBand and atrPctBand+crossSection -- and once offered it was chosen in nine quarters of nine, taking the out-of-sample result from $2300.28 at 13.39% to $2588.43 at 10.96%. Better on both axes in sample too, and it is the only change that has moved 2025.

readThisFirst: breakout + a 200-day MA trend gate is the first config to beat its own random-entry null by a detectable margin (p=0.005, excess 1.55R vs an MDE of 1.34R), and it does it at a 12.43% drawdown against BTC's 52.06%. It is still the best of 1152 in-sample configurations, so treat it as the thing to attack next, not as a finding. Everything before it -- long tpR, long maxHold -- was buying exposure in a rising market.

nextUp: Awaiting sp500.tar.gz. On arrival: install under its OWN root, read manifest.json FIRST and report departedRecovered and missingPct BEFORE any result -- if few of the failed companies resolved, the test is compromised and that must be said before a number is seen, not after. randomEntryNull.reading: The leader's entry rule is worth 0.0973R against a coin flip with identical geometry, and a random-entry account ends ABOVE it. No config's excess reaches what this test could detect, so the honest statement is not 'no edge' but 'no edge large enough to see through the noise a 100R target creates'.

breakout + ma200 gate (the leader).reading: The first configuration in this campaign whose excess over a matched-geometry random entry exceeds what the test can detect. It survives the harder version too: restricting the random entries to bars the 200-MA gate allows makes the excess LARGER, so the gate is not doing the work on its own. Caveat that has to stay attached: this is the best of ~1152 configurations searched on the same data, and at that many draws roughly 6 configs reach p<0.005 by chance. p=0.005 is not a discovery here, it is a reason to keep testing this one.

leveredLeader.reading: Not a better strategy, the same one levered 20x. A 94% drawdown means $1000 was worth about $60 at the low. Reported because the owner asked for the highest number; the drawdown is reported with it because the number is meaningless without it.

walkForward.runner: walkforward.mjs (node walkforward.mjs, ~2 min), pinned by walkforward.test.mjs
walkForward.construction: Each quarter of 2024-01-01..2026-03-31 is scored by parameters fitted only on bars that closed before it began. Nine quarters chained into one curve.

inSampleComparison.reading: +1.85R in-sample against +1.14R out-of-sample over the identical window. That gap is the size of the hindsight, measured rather than guessed: roughly 40% of the apparent edge was the search seeing the answer.

walkForward.parameterStability: trendMa 150 and minStopPct 0.03 and volTarget 0.05 chosen in ALL NINE quarters; beTriggerR 2.5 in seven of nine. The search is not chasing noise. Note it never picks the full-sample leader's trendMa 200.
walkForward.quarterlyShape: Four of nine quarters positive. The return is concentrated in 2024Q1 (+2.84R), 2024Q4 (+1.73R) and 2025Q3 (+2.90R) -- the same fat-tail dependence as the in-sample result.
walkForward.leaksStillPresent: This is NOT a clean holdout and must not be quoted as one. The grid was designed after seeing full-sample results; the universe was chosen after seeing all of it; and walkforward.mjs's FIXED block holds the entry mode, the filters, and the one-bar fill delay constant at values selected in-sample rather than refitting them. Refitting those too would be the stronger test and has not been run.

laterStarts.reading: This is the caveat that matters most. The whole out-of-sample result is three quarters out of nine -- 2024Q1, 2024Q4 and 2025Q3. The other six are negative. Restricted to 2025 the walk-forward is positive ONLY because of 2025Q3; four of its five quarters lose money. A book running this would have spent most of its time losing and made everything back in three quarters. That is the trade-level tail dependence showing up at the quarter level, and it is what trend following is -- but it means nobody should read $1974.68 as a steady climb.

refitEverything.what: Entry mode, fill delay and filters refitted every quarter alongside the numeric parameters, instead of held at in-sample values. 576 configs x 9 quarters.
refitEverything.vsRestricted: Better than the $1974.68 of the version that held those three constant. Removing the leak did not cost anything -- it helped.

whatItChose.entryDelayBars 1: ALL NINE quarters, on training data alone. The one-bar fill delay was not an in-sample spike; an independent search picks it every time.
whatItChose.entryMode breakout: eight of nine (anticipate once, in 2024Q2, which lost)
whatItChose.filters null: SEVEN OF NINE. A training-only search mostly DECLINES the filters, which confirms what the in-sample sweeps only hinted: they are noise, not signal.

refitEverything.stillFixed: What remains held at in-sample values is the structural frame, and it is not nothing: long-only, trendGate on in 'ma' mode, tpR 100, maxStopPct 0.20, alignMode none, lockBreakeven on, beLockR 0.2, volClamp 3. The trend gate in particular was chosen in-sample and is the single change that created this result.
refitEverything.quarterlyShape: Four of nine positive: 2024Q1 +2.84R, 2024Q3 +0.22R, 2024Q4 +3.53R, 2025Q3 +1.11R. The other five negative. Same concentration as every other cut of this result.

structuralRefit.what: Refit the structural frame too -- whether to gate at all, in which mode, and the target multiple -- not just the tuned numbers. 384 configs x 9 quarters.
structuralRefit.vsEarlier: Best walk-forward yet: $1974.68 (numbers only) -> $2249.27 (+ entry mode, delay, filters) -> $2300.28 (+ the structural frame). Every leak closed so far has made the result better, not worse.

whatItChose.tpR 100: eight of nine (tpR 12 once, in 2024Q2, which lost)

structuralRefit.reading: This is the strongest evidence in the campaign. A search that has never seen the quarter it is judged on converges on the same structure nine times out of nine -- INCLUDING on whether to apply the trend gate at all, which was the one choice most obviously made with hindsight. The gate is not an in-sample artifact.
structuralRefit.stillFixed: long-only, entryMode breakout, entryDelayBars 1, filters null, alignMode none (inert), maxStopPct 0.20, lockBreakeven, beLockR 0.2, volClamp 3. The first three were each chosen independently in 8/9 or 9/9 quarters by the previous refit, so holding them is now a recorded observation rather than an assumption.

fittingObjective.why: The walk-forward's fit function maximised final balance and nothing else. Given a choice between an unlimited book and one capped at three positions it took unlimited in all nine quarters, because more concurrent bets is more balance in-sample -- it never saw that unlimited got there through a 24% drawdown while the cap took 9%. The campaign's leader had been picked on drawdown TOO, so the walk-forward was being asked to validate a choice made on a criterion it did not share.
fittingObjective.fix: walkforward.mjs now takes objective 'balance' or 'mar' (balance per unit of drawdown). Both are reported.

mar.chose: maxConcurrent 2 @0.5% for four quarters, then unlimited @1% for five

fittingObjective.conclusion: The concurrency cap is NOT validated out of sample under either objective. Its large in-sample gain was hindsight.

btcRegimeOffered.chose: btcRegime 50 in nine quarters of nine under the balance objective, eight of nine under mar
btcRegimeOffered.progression: $1974.68 (numbers only) -> $2249.27 (+ entry mode, delay, filters) -> $2300.28 (+ structural frame) -> $2588.43 (+ btcRegime offered). Every step improved it.
btcRegimeOffered.lessonRecorded: The filters were reported as 'declined in 7 of 9 quarters'. That was true of the filters the grid CONTAINED. btcRegime alone was never in it. A component absent from a grid is not a component the search rejected, and the write-up did not distinguish those.

gridSizeIsAVariable.ladder: Four grid sizes, same fixed frame, same window, trendMa pinned at 150 so grid size is the only thing that varies.
gridSizeIsAVariable.finding: Grid size matters and there is an INTERIOR optimum, around eight points here. Eight beats two and it beats forty-eight and one hundred and ninety-two, on balance, drawdown and mean R alike.
gridSizeIsAVariable.correction: The previous commit claimed 'a bigger honest grid is a worse grid'. That is too strong and is withdrawn. It rested on one comparison, $2588.43 against $2387.26, which was partly confounded -- the small grid pinned trendMa at 150 while the large one swept it. With the confound removed the relationship is not monotone: 192 points beats 48, and 2 points loses to 8. The direction of the original observation survives for grids above the optimum; the general claim does not.
gridSizeIsAVariable.stabilityHypothesisRefuted: Choice stability, computed from training runs alone, does NOT rank grids. It flags the worst one -- medium at 0.778 -- but tiny and small both score a perfect 1.000 and differ by 13% in out-of-sample balance. It is a useful warning sign and not a selection criterion, and it was proposed here as the latter.
gridSizeIsAVariable.consequenceForTheLeader: None. The leader already comes from the eight-point grid, which the corrected ladder confirms is the best of the four.

bugsFound.cause: each quarter's run was truncated at the quarter end, amputating every position still open when the quarter closed. With 50-to-200-bar holds that is most of them, and the amputated part is the tail that carries a trend follower's return.
bugsFound.caught: by checking the same configurations held FIXED over the identical window, which scored +0.74R to +1.85R. A -0.42R result next to a +1.85R result for the same trades is not a finding, it is a bug.
bugsFound.fix: exits now run to the end of the data; only ENTRY dates are confined to the decision window. Letting a trade run its course after entry is not lookahead -- its exit rule was fixed when it was entered. Pinned by a test.

bugsFound.cause: `chose` was a hardcoded list of five keys rather than derived from the grid
bugsFound.impact: whether the entry mode and filters moved between quarters -- the entire question that run existed to answer -- was invisible in its own output
bugsFound.fix: chose is now derived from Object.keys(grid); pinned by a test

bugsFound.symptom: a sweep of four btcRegime periods returned four byte-identical rows for the short side
bugsFound.cause: entryGate was wired into the anticipate branch and the shared dip/breakout branch but not into bos, so every filters spec was silently ignored for that entry mode
bugsFound.fix: entryGate is now checked in all three branches and its refusals are tallied as reason externalGate; a test asserts a gate that refuses everything produces no trades in bos, breakout and anticipate alike

bugsFound.symptom: would have admitted shorts only into rising markets
bugsFound.cause: 'BTC above its own average' is a market-wide uptrend, applied unchanged to both directions -- the same bug class as backtest.js's trend gate
bugsFound.fix: direction-aware, with a test covering both directions against both a rising and a falling BTC

bugsFound.symptom: eight parameters accepted and silently ignored, each producing byte-identical rows that read as a swept axis
bugsFound.list: stopMode outside anticipate; alignMode outside bos/anticipate; the swing window for breakout; trailStartR below trailR; entryGate in the bos branch; chopFilter, requireHigherLow and minRoomR for breakout
bugsFound.fix: A capability table now declares which entry modes honour alignMode, chopFilter, requireHigherLow and minRoomR, and passing a RESTRICTIVE value to a mode that ignores it throws. Permissive values never throw -- alignMode 'none' asks for no alignment, which is exactly what an ignoring mode delivers, so it drops no claim and the whole campaign passes it. The signature default is accepted everywhere too, because omission and an explicit default cannot be told apart.

bugsFound.symptom: reported that stability does not predict performance AND that bigger grids do better -- the opposite of the previous commit
bugsFound.cause: trendMa was not in the ladder's FIXED block, so the two grids that did not SWEEP it fell back to backtest.js's default of 20 instead of the endorsed 150. The ladder measured 'was trendMa fitted at all', not grid size.
bugsFound.caught: the two smallest grids scoring far below every walk-forward already recorded, which no change in grid size could explain
bugsFound.fix: trendMa pinned at 150 in FIXED, with a comment saying why; ladder re-run

bugsFound.cause: the loader only validated `time`; parseFloat("") is NaN and every NaN comparison is false, so that bar would trigger neither a stop nor a target and simply be stepped over

bugsFound.symptom: CANDLE_COST_MODEL was set correctly and the first equities run still died saying no cost model was named

bugsFound.fix: resolved inside the function body; tests pin the null-call-site path for both

concurrency.measured: The unlimited book peaks at 19 simultaneous positions on 2024-12-03 and spends 26% of its time with 9 or more open. It is flat 20.4% of the time.
concurrency.whyItMatters: simulateEquity compounds trades one after another in entry order, which silently assumes the book is never long two things at once. It is. Sequential compounding cannot see correlated positions moving together, so every drawdown this campaign reported before this point is a FLOOR, not a measurement. maxConcurrent does not fix the accounting -- it constrains the book the way a real one is constrained, and declined signals are counted and reported rather than quietly dropped.
concurrency.stillUnmodelled: Positions are still compounded sequentially rather than marked to market together, so a correlated multi-position drawdown is still not directly measured.

equitiesBlocked.status: Cannot be tested in this container. Outbound HTTPS to public market-data hosts is denied by the environment's network policy -- the proxy gateway answers 403 to CONNECT for stooq.com and stooq.pl, confirmed in its own status endpoint.
equitiesBlocked.whatWouldUnblockIt: Equities daily bars supplied the same way the crypto bundle was: a tar.gz of per-symbol CSVs with time,open,high,low,close,volume. bundle-loader.mjs reads that format already and nothing else would need to change.
equitiesBlocked.whyItMatters: The owner named equities as the actual target. FINDINGS.md's own equities section is a warning about this exact failure mode -- an apparent edge that turned out to be the window's payoff geometry.

decayDiagnosis.question: Is the leader's decline (2023 +2.92R, 2024 +2.01R, 2025 +0.21R, 2026 -0.94R) the strategy dying or the market going quiet?
decayDiagnosis.answer: BOTH, and that is a better answer than either alone. What a RANDOM long entry earned under the same geometry fell from +0.76R to -0.86R -- no strategy choice can explain that, the trend simply stopped being there. But the strategy's EXCESS over random fell too, from +2.16R to +0.27R to -0.08R. So the market got harder AND the edge over a coin flip shrank.
decayDiagnosis.theSharpPoint: In 2025 the strategy beat a random entry by 0.27R. The campaign's own power analysis puts the smallest excess this test can detect at roughly 1.3-1.5R. In 2025 the strategy is not distinguishable from a coin flip.
decayDiagnosis.notAnArtefact: Checked at stop widths of 4%, 6%, 10% and 15%. The level of the random-entry return moves; the year ordering never does.
decayDiagnosis.sideNote: The efficiency ratio barely moved (0.171 to 0.146, a 17% range). What collapsed was the DIRECTION of the moves, not their straightness -- 2025-26 crypto was no choppier, it just stopped going up.

shortSide.fullPeriod: Loses in all 99 configurations swept. Best $816.25, a 18.4% loss, at a 49.38% drawdown.
shortSide.theInterestingPart: Shorts are POSITIVE in 2024 and 2025 -- 2025 being exactly the year the long side collapsed to +0.21R. The two sides are complementary in time.

combined.verdict: Combining makes it worse on both axes. The short side's 2023 losses (-0.50R over 110 trades) outweigh its 2024-25 gains.

shortSide.theHandicapThatMattersAndIsNotResolved: The engine implements shorts for entryMode 'bos' only and on the base stop/target/timeout path alone -- no breakeven lock, no trailing stop, no partials. The long side's result depends materially on the breakeven lock (beTriggerR 3, chosen by the walk-forward in nine quarters of nine), so the short side is being judged with a worse exit engine than the long side. The measured gap is far too large for the lock to close (-18% against +1575%), so the conclusion 'shorts do not rescue this' stands -- but 'shorts do not work' is NOT established and would need the short exit path built first.
shortSide.engineChange: backtest.js's trend gate is now direction-aware. Both gate conditions describe an uptrend; applied unchanged to a short they permitted selling only into rising markets, which is worse than no gate at all. Two tests pin both directions.
shortSide.engineNowComplete: trailR, trailStartR, partialAtR, partialFrac, trailingTpPct, lockBreakeven and exitOnSwingHigh are all mirrored for shorts. Only two ENTRY-side conditions remain long-only and they are genuinely unwritten rather than untested: requireHigherLow (a rising sequence of swing lows) and minRoomR (clear air above entry, measured by a nearestResAbove with no nearestSupportBelow counterpart).
shortSide.verdictUpgraded: Previously recorded as 'shorts do not rescue this, but shorts do not work is NOT established' because the short side was being judged with a worse exit engine. It is now judged with the same one and the answer does not move: the short side loses on this data. The handicap was not the explanation.
shortSide.whyItStillMattered: The engine capability is the deliverable. The owner wants the short path for EQUITIES, where a two-sided book is the normal construction rather than an afterthought.

equitiesReadiness.formatGivenToOwner: candle-bundle/1440/<SYMBOL>.csv, header time,open,high,low,close,volume, time in unix seconds, oldest row first. bundle-loader.mjs reads it unchanged.
equitiesReadiness.whatWasHardcoded: Three call sites assumed XBTUSD was the market: benchmark.mjs's headline row, campaign.mjs's btcRegime series, and robustness.mjs's copy of it. On an equities bundle the benchmark would have printed 'BTC $n/a' next to every leaderboard and the btcRegime filter would have refused to compile with a message about BTC. Two of the three would have gone quiet, which is how the other eight silent no-ops in this campaign got as far as they did.
equitiesReadiness.fix: bundle-loader.marketProxy resolves it from the universe against an ordered candidate list -- XBTUSD, SPY, VOO, IVV, ^GSPC, QQQ -- honours an explicit override or CANDLE_MARKET_PROXY, and THROWS when it cannot resolve, naming what it looked for. benchmarks() now returns proxySymbol/proxy/proxyMaxDrawdownPct instead of btc/btcMaxDrawdownPct, because a field called 'btc' on an equities run is a lie even when the number is right.
stillToDoWhenDataArrives: declare survivorship bias unless the bundle demonstrably includes delisted names
confirm with the owner whether prices are split/dividend adjusted -- adjustment changes historical stop distances, and stop distance is the variable this whole campaign turned on
rename btcRegime to marketRegime once it is used on a second asset class
runOrder: robustness.mjs with the crypto-fitted leader untouched (the honest transfer test)
walkforward.mjs with an EIGHT-point grid (the corrected ladder's optimum)
only then sweep, and stop early

costModel.built: costs.mjs. Named models with sourced numbers: krakenTaker (0.008/0.0005, what every crypto result here was computed under), usEquityRetail (0/0.0005), usEquityIbkr (0.00005/0.0005), and zeroCost as a labelled diagnostic.
costModel.whyItRefusesToGuess: A crypto universe defaults to krakenTaker so existing results stay reproducible. Anything else must be named. The failure mode of guessing is not a slightly wrong number: at a 3% stop crypto pays 0.57R a trade and US equities pay 0.033R, so equities charged Kraken rates would look like a dead strategy and crypto charged equity rates would manufacture an edge. costFor() throws on an unrecognised universe and the message says so.
costModel.identity: costInR(model, stopPct) = 2*(feeRate+slipPct)/stopPct. Pinned by a test against the two figures the campaign turned on: 1.70R at a 1% stop, 0.11R at 15%.
costModel.verified: The leader reproduces byte-identically after the rewiring -- 182 trades, $20,949.34, 20.77%.

equities.bundle: equity-bundle/1440, 30 symbols (10 sector/index ETFs + 20 large caps), 920 daily bars each, 2023-01-03 to 2026-09-02. Raw unadjusted OHLC from yfinance via Colab. Held in a SEPARATE root from candle-bundle so the two universes can never be mixed.
equities.costModel: usEquityRetail — 0 commission, 5bp per-leg slippage. Named explicitly; costFor() refused to run until it was.

transferTest.what: The crypto-fitted leader, not one parameter changed, run on equities.

THE_RESULT.reading: $15,873 is the UNIVERSE, not the strategy. A random entry on the same 30 symbols with the same stop distances, target, hold and cost earns 0.5751R against the strategy's 0.5814R. The excess is 0.0064R at p=0.47 -- a coin flip. It fails the harder gated-bar version too. Thirty of today's mega caps and sector ETFs over 2023-2026 make money almost however you enter them; the equal-weight basket alone returns $2,646.
THE_RESULT.whyTheDollarsMislead: A random-entry ACCOUNT computed as 1000*(1+0.01*0.5751)^252 lands near $4,242, which invites the reading that the strategy's $15,873 beat it. It does not: that formula is a crude geometric approximation with no volatility targeting and no path ordering, so it is not like-for-like. The rigorous comparison is mean R per trade, and there the two are the same number.

equities.selectionBiasConfirmed: This was flagged as a caveat before the run and the null turned it into the explanation. The symbol list was 30 currently-listed large caps chosen by me — NVDA at $15,676 buy-and-hold is in it and the companies that failed are not. Survivorship-free equities data (Norgate, Sharadar, CRSP) is the only way to test this properly and it is a paid source.

subgroupDiagnostic.whyItIsWorthRunning: The matched-geometry null draws from the same symbols in the same proportions, so it already controls for the universe being a basket of winners. That conclusion -- no detectable edge -- stands on its own and survivorship does not undermine it. What survivorship DOES remove is the thing a trend gate is for: the chance to avoid a name that falls and keeps falling.
subgroupDiagnostic.reading: Directionally consistent: on names that only rose, the strategy is WORSE than random -- its stop-outs are pure drag. On the laggards, random entry earns almost nothing (+0.0225R) and the strategy earns +0.3871R.
whyItIsNotAFinding: the excess of 0.3646R is BELOW the 0.696R this test could detect at 80% power
the split is POST-HOC -- subgroups defined by an outcome only knowable at the end, so it is not tradeable as stated
two subgroups tested, so even the nominal p carries a multiplicity cost
subgroupDiagnostic.prereg: EQUITIES-LAGGARD-EXCESS-2026-09, registry ledger seq 15, registered before any survivorship-free data exists so the prediction cannot be reshaped once it does.

survivorshipFreeRoute.correction: Recorded because it was stated the other way earlier: a survivorship-free universe was called a paid product. Partly wrong. The bulk of the reconstruction is free and mechanical; only the departed names are.
survivorshipFreeRoute.whatWorks: Wikipedia's constituents table carries a Date-added column, so every current member that JOINED after 2023-01-01 is removed by rule -- roughly sixty companies that entered the index because they did well. No judgement involved.
survivorshipFreeRoute.whatDoesNot: The 'Selected changes' table that listed REMOVALS is gone from that page. Verified 2026-09-04: it returns two tables and the second is a navbox. So the departed names are hand-supplied from recall, the list is incomplete, and its incompleteness is the residual survivorship bias. The manifest reports how many resolved, which bounds what got in but not what was never listed.
survivorshipFreeRoute.standing: Better than a hand-picked basket of winners, worse than a vendor point-in-time file. Results must be labelled that way and not called survivorship-free.
survivorshipFreeRoute.debugHistory: Three scripts failed before this one and the useful lesson is about diagnosis, not Wikipedia: v1 and v2 used a `!pip` cell magic that is a SyntaxError when the file is run rather than pasted, so nothing executed and nothing printed -- a silent failure indistinguishable from several other causes. v3 removed the magic and printed a checkpoint per step, which located the real fault in one run.

acceptanceCriterion.asStated: ~10 trades a month, win rate at or above 40%, wins large enough to offset the losses.
acceptanceCriterion.met: Yes, on every count, by the current equities candidate: 5.7 trades/month, 40.5% win rate, 2.92R average win against a 1.01R average loss, expectancy +0.5814R.
acceptanceCriterion.andAlsoMetBy: A RANDOM ENTRY using the same exits: 42.8% win rate -- HIGHER than the strategy -- with a 2.67 payoff and +0.5589R expectancy. That is the whole problem with the criterion as an acceptance test.
acceptanceCriterion.whyTheShapeIsFree: A wide stop with no reachable take-profit and a bounded hold caps the loss near 1R and lets winners run past 3R. A ~40% win rate at a ~2.7 payoff is therefore a property of the EXIT geometry, not the entry, and it comes free with any long entry in a rising market. Breakeven at a 2.89:1 payoff is a 25.7% win rate, so 40% clears it with room -- and so does the coin flip's 42.8%.

whatFrequencyCosts.reading: Low frequency does not reduce risk, it buys noise. Ten trades a month needs about three years to confirm a half-R edge and over a decade for a quarter-R one, before any allowance for same-day clustering.

failed.sample_sufficient: effective n 175 against 882 required to detect a quarter-R edge

gateVerdict.reading: Four conditions green including the owner's own criterion. It fails on the two that decide whether the result is real.
